title: What history teaches
tomorrow: Year three close: the people and their story

cards: History doesn't hand out lessons by itself. People draw them, and not always the same ones. The same hard years can teach one family to hold on tighter and another to start over somewhere new.

So today isn't a verdict on the Jewish story. It's a look at a few threads that keep turning up in it, through kings and exiles, study halls and new countries, and the Shoah, which the year approached with care.
Five of them, and one sentence that holds them together.

teach.b: The first two belong together: surviving and remembering. Again and again this year, the people outlived the powers that tried to end them, partly by refusing to forget. Zachor.
A yahrzeit candle on the right date. A story told to the children. The third is adapting.

When the Temple was about to fall, the Talmud tells that Yochanan ben Zakkai was carried out of besieged Jerusalem and asked the Roman commander for one thing: Yavneh and its sages. A place to keep teaching.
With the altar gone, Jewish life was rebuilt around study, prayer and the family table. The form changed so the heart could stay. The fourth is arguing.

The houses of Hillel and Shammai argued for so long that the Talmud tells of a voice from heaven settling it: these and these are the words of the living God, and the law follows Hillel, in part because Hillel's students were gentle and put the other side's words before their own.
Argument, in this story, isn't a crack in the tradition. It's part of how the tradition lives.
The fifth is hoping. Prayers that faced Jerusalem. Next year.
Od lo avdah tikvatenu, our hope is not yet lost. None of these five is a victory lap; this year never pretended the story was all triumph.
But side by side they spell out a sentence sometimes sung as a song, am Yisrael chai, the people of Israel lives.
Or, as today's line puts it plainly: we are still here.

how: Jews return to their history in the yearly cycle of fasts and festivals, at the Seder, on memorial days and in study, and the phrase am Yisrael chai, the people of Israel lives, is sung at gatherings of different kinds.

games.why: the Talmud tells that he asked for Yavneh and its sages. with the Temple gone, Jewish life was rebuilt around study and prayer.

practice: Look back over this year's story, or your own family's history, or both, and ask what it actually taught you, not what it's supposed to teach.
Find three things, a few words each, counting them on your fingers if you like: maybe one about losing something, one about starting again, one that surprises you.
If you pray, give thanks for the people who carried the story this far.
